title: Pirc Defence | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: A ten-minute game, and we're climbing — rated sixteen-seventy-three now. Black plays d6, which could be a Pirc or a Caro depending on what follows.
We grab the full center with d4.
d6 and c6 — this flexible system exists; Black usually follows with the knight to f6 to transpose into some kind of Pirc.
Our strategy is no different from usual — the knight to c3, developing and holding the center.
Black plays g6, and now it's a Pirc with an early c6, a perfectly viable continuation.
How to arrange our pieces? There's no single right answer — the bishop to b3, the bishop to c4 — but I like f4, planning the knight to f3, especially against this early c6.
Black fianchettoes with the bishop to g7, and we bring the knight to f3, supporting the big center.
Black develops the other bishop to g4, pinning our knight on f3 — double-bishop development aiming at our center.
We develop with an eye toward defending d4 and that pinned knight — the bishop to e3.
Black plays the queen to b6, a theoretical thrust hitting b2 and pressuring d4.
The theoretical reply, as far as I remember, is the queen to d2 — now if Black snatches on b2, we're ready to meet it.
Black takes on f3, and we recapture with the g-pawn. Yes, we have doubled pawns, but it's really no big deal — it opens the g-file straight at Black's kingside, which could benefit us.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We castle queenside. Not h4 yet — that's too early, since we don't even know where Black is going to castle.
Black castles kingside, and now we can start thinking about a kingside attack.
h4 is a great move here, but it's not the only way to shatter Black's king position — we can also use the f-pawn and play f5 first, prying it open so h4 lands even harder later.
Black plays the queen to c7.
Now h4, cranking up maximal pressure on the g6-pawn.
Black seeks counterplay with b5.
We push h5, and notice I'm completely ignoring Black's queenside — his attack there simply isn't fast enough.
Black plays b4, poking our knight.
Where should the knight go? It doesn't have many squares, but the knight to e2 is ideal — it's rerouting toward f4.
Black develops the knight to d7. It temporarily blocks in a bishop, but that's only temporary — pieces will reshuffle.
We take, h takes g6, also eyeing the e6-square that gets weak once the f7-pawn is pried away.
Black recaptures on g6, and we take again with the f-pawn.
Black recaptures once more, and the knight completes its journey to f4 — a beautiful, devastating outpost right next to the king.
Black's king crawls to f7 with literally no squares, and our queen is ready to pour into the attack.
Stay attentive to all the squares you have access to — it's a simple enough attack, which is exactly why I don't really recommend this line for Black.
Replaying it: c6, the knight to c3, g6.
f4, the bishop to g4, the knight to f3, the bishop to g7 — a legitimate line Black played, but not a very good one.
The bishop to e3, the queen to b6, the queen to d2.
Black took on f3 and developed the knight to f6 — and according to the opening explorer, the knight to f6 here is already inaccurate.
Most people play the knight to d7 instead.
The knight to d7 is the main move.
And after we castle queenside, ninety-one games continued from here.
The queen to a5, planning a quick b5-b4 — Black has to get things moving on the queenside, because if he procrastinates you saw what happens to him.
This whole line is very dubious for Black; our center is monstrous, and we can just play the king to b1 for safety.
Black plays b5.
And we simply start our own attack with h4. Grabbing on b2 is never a good idea for Black — not outright losing, but very dubious.
The rook wants that open file toward the king, whereas the queen alone is not a very effective attacker, so parking it on b2 to munch a pawn is a mistake.
This could have been an eleven-move game — it just shows how those b2-pawn grabs come back to haunt you.
d4 and c6 — the win is very straightforward once we land the knight on f4, with too many weak squares and pawns for Black to defend.
f4, g6, the knight to c3.
The bishop to g7. Do you ever play f4 and then e5?
The knight to f3, the knight to f6 — normally you wait for Black to commit the knight to f6.
Then e5 is even a move here, though a little premature — generally you develop your minor pieces first before pushing e5.
